ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gynecologic Oncology Referral — Ada Lovelace — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for abnormal bleeding and pelvic pain: history, speculum examination and cervical biopsy, blood count and iron studies, conversion of opium tincture to measured oral morphine, an iron infusion, and a gynecologic oncology referral

text.paragraph: Friable exophytic cervical mass with five months of abnormal bleeding and constant pelvic pain in a 35-year-old woman, biopsied today, with iron deficiency anemia. Please confirm the diagnosis, stage the disease, advise on treatment intent and options, and help with control of bleeding and pain. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks; pathology expected within a week. [S]

list.item: What is the diagnosis, and what further staging is needed?
Is the intent of treatment curative or palliative, and what treatment do you recommend?
How should the bleeding be controlled?
Which tumor or genetic tests are needed?
How should her pain and long-term opioid therapy be managed during treatment?
When should palliative care be involved?

text.paragraph: Mathematician, 35, with five months of bleeding between periods and after intercourse, heavier periods, a watery blood-stained discharge, and a constant pelvic ache, average 7 of 10. She has taken prescribed opium tincture, 0.5 mL four to six times a day and measured at times with a household spoon, for about two years for recurrent pelvic and abdominal pain; today it was changed to measured oral morphine solution 5 mg every 4 hours as needed, with acetaminophen, laxatives and naloxone. No opioid use disorder on assessment. Earlier history of measles in childhood, cholera in her early twenties, and chronic ill health with asthma and digestive problems. Never smoked. On speculum examination a 5 cm friable exophytic mass replaces the cervix and bleeds on contact; on bimanual and rectovaginal examination the left parametrium feels thickened, not reaching the sidewall. Punch biopsy and HPV typing sent. Hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, mean cell volume 74 fL, ferritin 5 ng/mL, platelets 412; creatinine 0.68 mg/dL; ALT 18 U/L; albumin 3.6 g/dL; serum hCG negative. First intravenous iron infusion given today. PHQ-9 8. She wants to be told everything directly and to make her own decisions, and she wants to keep her mind clear for her work [S]

list.item: She wants to know plainly what the bleeding means and to make her own decisions. [S]
She wants her mornings clear-headed for her mathematical work and fears that stronger pain medicine will cloud her mind. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Augusta Ada Byron was born on December 10, 1815, in Piccadilly, London, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Byron. [D]
She was often ill as a child. In 1829, at 13, she caught measles, from which she took a long while to recover; she was bedridden for a whole year. [D]
On July 8, 1835, she married William King, who was created an earl in 1838, making her Countess of Lovelace. [D]
Her health suffered after a bout of cholera in 1837, and she had lingering problems with asthma and her digestive system. [D]
Her doctors gave her painkillers such as laudanum and opium; she reportedly had mood swings and hallucinations. [D]

Between 1842 and 1843 she translated L. F. Menabrea's article on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and added her own extensive Notes, published in 1843 under the initials A.A.L. The Notes, which include a method for computing Bernoulli numbers on the engine, are often described as the first published computer program. [D]

Her health, always fragile, declined sharply after 1843. By the end of that year she was taking several medicines for different health problems; in 1844 she wrote that a recent illness had left her 'utterly unable to think even of my studies', and she thought of writing a scientific study of the effects of opium and wine based on her own experience. In the 1840s she had what she called heart or rheumatic attacks. [D]
Gambling on horses was a passion of her later years, and she pawned some of her jewels to finance it. [D]
By 1851 she was extremely sick with uterine cancer. [D]

list.item: Bleeding between periods and after intercourse, with heavier periods, a watery blood-stained discharge and a constant pelvic ache, for about five months; average pain 7 of 10 despite her opium tincture; a friable cervical mass found on examination and biopsied; cause not yet established at intake: active, confirmed [S]
Iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, mean cell volume 74 fL, ferritin 5 ng/mL, with tiredness and breathlessness on stairs: active, confirmed [S]

Long-term prescribed opioid therapy: opium tincture for recurrent pelvic and abdominal pain for about two years, measured at times with a household spoon, converted at intake to measured oral morphine; no opioid use disorder on a DSM-5 assessment; naloxone supplied: active, confirmed [S]

Stop opium tincture and change to measured oral morphine solution 5 mg every 4 hours as needed with an oral syringe, with acetaminophen, senna and polyethylene glycol, a naloxone nasal spray, a prescription monitoring check, locked storage, one prescriber, and review in two weeks. Guideline: Use of Opioids for Adults With Pain From Cancer or Cancer Treatment: ASCO Guideline (Paice JA, et al. J Clin Oncol 2023;41:914-930) (2023); CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (Dowell D, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep 2022;71(RR-3):1-95) (2022) [S]

Iron deficiency anemia: ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg intravenously today and in two weeks, with a blood count at each visit and ferritin 6 to 8 weeks after the infusions. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia monograph (2026) [S]

Blood tests: blood count, ferritin, creatinine, ALT, albumin and a pregnancy test; HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C tests before any cancer treatment; PHQ-9. Guideline: Hepatitis B Virus Screening and Management for Patients With Cancer Prior to Therapy: ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion Update (Hwang JP, et al. J Clin Oncol 2020;38:3698-3715) (2020); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
